t: Beautiful Pairs — Closest Pair under Manhattan Distance
o: Find the index pair minimizing Manhattan distance |dx|+|dy|, breaking ties by lexicographically smallest index pair. Brute force is O(n²) — too slow for n = 1e5. The classical trick: with u = x+y and v = x−y, Manhattan distance equals max(|Δu|, |Δv|) (Chebyshev distance in rotated coordinates), letting us adapt the standard divide-and-conquer closest-pair algorithm: sort by x, recurse on halves, and check a narrow strip sorted by u with early breaking. Ties are resolved by carrying (distance, min-index, max-index) triples and comparing lexicographically.
k: Manhattan distance transforms to Chebyshev distance via u = x+y, v = x−y, unlocking the closest-pair D&C algorithm.
Strip pruning (points within current best distance of the dividing line, scanned in u-order with early break) keeps the algorithm near O(n log n).
Tie-breaking by original index pair requires comparing (d, min(i,j), max(i,j)) triples, not just distances.

a.i: Check all pairs, keeping the best (distance, i, j) triple. O(n²) — only viable for tiny inputs, but establishes the tie-break semantics.
s: Compare (d, min(i,j), max(i,j)) against the best triple.

a.n: Approach 2: Divide and conquer closest pair (rotated metric)
a.i: Sort point indices by (x, y). Recursively solve halves; combine by collecting points within current best distance of the midline, sorting them by u = x+y, and testing each against subsequent strip points while the u-gap is below the best distance (early break). Candidate comparison uses the (d, lo-index, hi-index) triple so ties resolve lexicographically.
s: Sort indices by x then y; define cand(i,j) updating the best triple.
Recursion base: brute force when ≤ 4 points.
Recurse on halves; gather strip points with |x − mid_x| < best, sort by u, scan with early break.
a.t: O(n log² n) — recursion with a per-level strip sort; with merged sorting this drops toward O(n log n)
a.sp: O(n) — sorted index arrays and strips per level

w: Explain the coordinate rotation identity first — it is the crux. Pitfalls: tie-breaking must use original indices (the sorted order scrambles them), and duplicate points (distance 0) must be handled naturally by the triple comparison. Follow-up: k closest pairs, or closest pair under pure Chebyshev/Euclidean metrics.
